newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bankgesellschaft merger possible, profit down.
newsitem.headline: Bankgesellschaft merger possible, profit down.

text.p: Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG, Germany's sixth-largest bank, said on Wednesday a tie-up with Norddeutsche Landesbank was possible but that it would take years as many difficult issues had to be resolved.

Bankgesellschaft also reported a 32.4 percent slide in operating profit in the first nine months of 1996, caused by galloping costs, high risk provisions and a 56 million-mark ($36.8 million) loss from own-account trading.

In a move that fuelled speculation of mergers in Germany's overcrowded bank sector, the two banks last month got approval from their owners -- Berlin, Lower Saxony and two east German states -- to intensify talks about closer co-operation.

"A legal link-up of the two big banking groups requires that additional business advantages can evolve from it," Hubertus Moser, one of two chief executives on the management board, told the bank's nine-month news conference.
"We are sure that this can be the case if certain preconditions are met about which we are in talks with our colleagues at NordLB. But we are under no time pressure."
A merger would create one of Germany's biggest banking groups with assets of over 500 billion marks ($328.4 billion).
Moser said the two banks should come with concrete proposals within the next six months but that it would take several years to complete a tie-up, which would require the approval of four states.
Bankgesellschaft is 56.8 percent owned by the state of Berlin. NordLB is 40 percent owned by Lower Saxony, with Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern owning an additional 10 percent each.
Sensitive issues concerning managerial control and the location of a merged group's investment banking business had to be discussed, Moser said.

But analysts see limited scope for synergy benefits and speculate that the real motivation for a tie-up is to replenish depleted state coffers. Pooling state ownership of the banks would allow a big sale of shares to the private sector.

Outlining Bankgesellschaft's nine-month results, Moser said operating profit after risk provisions fell to 465 million marks from 688 million. The decline is in stark contrast to sharp earnings gains at other major German banks.

But he predicted an improvement in earnings in the final quarter and a return to a trading profit for the full year. The shares responded by rising 0.75 marks or three percent to close at 26.20 marks, outperforming the market.
Moser held out the prospect for better profits in 1997 but declined to make a dividend forecast. The bank has said that a dividend rise would be possible for 1997 at the earliest.

The bank had been hurt by a slump in its home region of Berlin and Brandenburg which showed no signs of abating, Moser said. That explained why net risk provisions rose 12.9 percent to 612 million marks and would remain high.
Hit by a downturn in the real estate market, Berlin's economy has fared worse than all other German regions this year with firms collapsing at a rate far above the national average.
In addition, the bank is still grappling with the cost of expanding its investment banking business and of melding the three Berlin banking groups from which it was formed in 1994.
But it said the rise in administration costs should slow down from the 14.3 percent rise in the first nine months.
Meanwhile the bank said it remained interested in buying an asset management firm and had contacted several prospective candidates in London and the U.S.
Net interest income rose 11.5 percent to 2.8 billion marks while net commission income rose 14.5 percent to 505 million.
The balance sheet total grew 12 percent to 315 billion marks while lending was up 8.1 percent at 217 billion. ($ = 1.522 German Marks)
